title: Whisper: Timing the Transient Execution to Leak Secrets and Break KASLR
problem: Transient execution vulnerabilities enable side-channel attacks that leak secrets and break KASLR even under kernel protections like KPTI and FLARE. Existing mitigations do not adequately defend against timing-based covert channels exploiting transient execution differences.
motivation: Breaking KASLR is critical for system security as it compromises kernel isolation and enables attackers to leak sensitive kernel memory and mounted defenses.
method: Whisper exploits timing differences in CPU transient execution (speculatively-run instructions that might be discarded)—an approach called Transient Execution Timing or TET. Using the Performance Monitor Unit (PMU), hardware counters in CPUs that track execution metrics, the authors measure these timing differences at the architectural level (without needing physical access) to infer secrets. They adapt three known attack techniques (Meltdown, Zombieload, and Spectre-RSB) to use TET, showing how to break KASLR (the security feature that randomizes kernel memory locations). Because existing kernel and hardware protections focus on blocking other types of information leakage, they don't adequately defend against TET-based attacks.
key_novelty: Whisper's core innovation is using execution timing differences in transient execution as an architectural-level covert channel (hidden extraction path) that reliably bypasses existing kernel and hardware security protections.
contributions: Novel Transient Execution Timing (TET) side channel (Whisper) based on execution time differences
TET implementations of Meltdown, Zombieload, and Spectre-RSB attacks
TET-KASLR attack breaking KASLR under KPTI and FLARE protection
Root cause analysis with PMU-based toolset and defense discussion

metrics.other: Successful attacks on multiple x86-64 CPU variants; KASLR bypassed
